subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which two products of the light-dependent reactions are required by the Calvin cycle?
questions.explain: The Calvin cycle uses ATP for energy and reduced NADP to reduce GP to triose phosphate.

questions.q: In the Calvin cycle, what is the role of ATP and reduced NADP in converting GP to triose phosphate (TP)?
options: ATP provides energy and reduced NADP provides hydrogen to reduce GP to TP
ATP oxidises GP while NADP fixes carbon
They regenerate RuBP directly from CO2
questions.explain: GP is reduced to triose phosphate using energy from ATP and hydrogen from reduced NADP.

questions.q: When using random quadrats to estimate the abundance of a species in a large field, why must the quadrats be placed randomly?
options: To avoid bias so the sample fairly represents the whole area
questions.explain: Random placement avoids sampling bias, giving an estimate that fairly represents the whole study area.

questions.q: The enzyme RuBisCO can also catalyse a reaction between RuBP and oxygen. What is the effect of this when CO2 levels are very low?
options: It increases the rate of glucose synthesis
It reduces the efficiency of carbon fixation
questions.explain: When CO2 is scarce, RuBisCO fixes oxygen instead, wastefully reducing the efficiency of the Calvin cycle.

questions.q: Out of every six molecules of triose phosphate (TP) made in the Calvin cycle, how many are used to regenerate RuBP?
questions.explain: Five of every six TP molecules are recycled to regenerate RuBP, leaving one to contribute to carbohydrate.

questions.q: In which part of the chloroplast do the light-dependent reactions take place?
questions.explain: The light-dependent reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes, where the photosystems are embedded.

questions.q: During the oxidation of triose phosphate to pyruvate in glycolysis, what is reduced?
questions.explain: As triose phosphate is oxidised, NAD accepts hydrogen to become reduced NAD, which can later feed the electron transport chain.

questions.q: Why does the light-dependent stage stop producing ATP when the Calvin cycle is blocked, for example by lack of CO2?
options: ADP and NADP are not regenerated and returned to the light reactions
questions.explain: If the Calvin cycle halts, ADP and NADP are not regenerated, so the light reactions run short of substrates for ATP and reduced NADP.

questions.q: What is the NET yield of ATP from one molecule of glucose during glycolysis alone?
questions.explain: Four ATP are produced but two are invested in the early phosphorylation steps, giving a net gain of two ATP.

questions.q: When CO2 is fixed onto the 5-carbon RuBP, what is the immediate product?
questions.explain: The unstable 6-carbon intermediate splits at once into two 3-carbon molecules of GP.

questions.q: A crop fixes 30,000 kJ per m2 per yr (NPP). A primary consumer assimilates 4,500 kJ per m2 per yr. What is the percentage efficiency of energy transfer?
Why does reduced FAD ultimately lead to the synthesis of fewer ATP molecules than reduced NAD?
options: FAD carries no electrons, only protons
FAD donates its electrons at a later point on the chain, pumping fewer protons
FAD is produced only in the cytoplasm
FAD is not used by the electron transport chain
questions.explain: FAD feeds electrons in further along the chain than NAD, so fewer protons are pumped and less ATP is made.

questions.q: In the carbon cycle, which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis fixes atmospheric CO2 into organic compounds, removing it from the air.

questions.q: What is the role of saprobiotic (decomposer) bacteria and fungi in ammonification?
options: They release nitrogen gas from nitrate
They convert nitrogen-containing compounds in dead matter into ammonium ions
questions.explain: Decomposers break down proteins and other nitrogen compounds in dead organisms, releasing ammonium ions.

questions.q: Why does a lack of oxygen quickly halt the entire electron transport chain?
options: Oxygen directly makes ATP from ADP
Without a final acceptor, electrons cannot move along the chain and carriers stay reduced
Oxygen is needed to phosphorylate glucose
questions.explain: With no oxygen to accept electrons at the end, the carriers remain reduced and the whole chain backs up and stops.

questions.q: How does anaerobic fermentation in yeast differ from that in mammalian muscle?
options: Yeast produces ethanol and CO2; muscle produces lactate
Both produce ethanol but only muscle releases CO2
Yeast uses oxygen whereas muscle does not
Yeast produces lactate; muscle produces ethanol
questions.explain: Yeast decarboxylates pyruvate and reduces it to ethanol, releasing CO2, whereas mammalian muscle forms lactate.

questions.q: Why does a very high temperature reduce the rate of the light-independent reactions?
options: It increases CO2 solubility too much
It stops light absorption by chlorophyll
It denatures enzymes such as RuBisCO
questions.explain: Excessive heat denatures the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, including RuBisCO, slowing the reactions.

questions.q: In which cellular location does glycolysis occur, and which type of phosphorylation produces its ATP?
questions.explain: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and generates ATP directly by substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence of conversions during nitrification?
options: Nitrogen gas then ammonia then nitrate
questions.explain: Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonia to nitrite (Nitrosomonas) and then nitrite to nitrate (Nitrobacter).

questions.q: Why is conserving genetic diversity within a species important for its long-term survival?
options: It removes the need for habitats
It guarantees a constant population size
It increases the chance that some individuals can survive environmental change or disease
questions.explain: Greater genetic variation means some individuals are more likely to possess alleles allowing survival when conditions change.

questions.q: Besides reduced NAD, what TWO products result from the link reaction per pyruvate molecule?
options: Acetyl coenzyme A and carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Each pyruvate is decarboxylated and combined with coenzyme A to form acetyl CoA, releasing CO2 and reducing NAD.

questions.q: Which feature of the chloroplast increases the surface area available for the light-dependent reactions?
options: The stacked thylakoid membranes forming grana
questions.explain: Thylakoids stacked into grana give a large membrane surface area for photosystems and electron carriers.

questions.q: Which describes a density-independent factor affecting a population?
options: Disease spread in a crowded population
A severe frost killing organisms regardless of population size
questions.explain: A frost affects the same proportion of individuals whatever the density, so it is density-independent.

questions.q: Where in the cell does the link reaction take place?
questions.explain: After pyruvate is actively transported into the mitochondrion, the link reaction occurs in the matrix.

questions.q: How is ATP generated during the light-dependent reactions?
options: By the direct action of light on ADP
By chemiosmosis as protons flow through ATP synthase in the thylakoid membrane
By substrate-level phosphorylation in the stroma
questions.explain: Protons accumulate in the thylakoid space and flow back through ATP synthase, driving photophosphorylation by chemiosmosis.

questions.q: Energy transferred to a trophic level is 50,000 kJ per m2 per yr and that passed on to the next level is 5,000 kJ per m2 per yr. What is the percentage efficiency of transfer?
A respiratory substrate gives a respiratory quotient (RQ) of about 0.7. Which substrate is most likely being respired?
questions.explain: Lipids are highly reduced and require more oxygen relative to CO2 produced, giving an RQ around 0.7.

questions.q: In one turn of the Krebs cycle, how many molecules of reduced NAD, reduced FAD and ATP are produced respectively?
questions.explain: Each Krebs turn yields three reduced NAD, one reduced FAD and one ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.q: According to the chemiosmotic theory, what directly drives ATP synthesis during oxidative phosphorylation?
options: Reduction of NAD by dehydrogenase enzymes
Direct transfer of a phosphate from a substrate
Movement of protons down their electrochemical gradient through ATP synthase
questions.explain: Protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, and this flux powers the phosphorylation of ADP.

questions.q: What is the approximate respiratory quotient (RQ) for the complete aerobic respiration of a carbohydrate such as glucose?
questions.explain: For glucose the volumes of CO2 produced and O2 consumed are equal, giving an RQ of 1.0.
